prompt: `TwoWeeks` calls `useWeek('2026-10-19')` twice, and its button calls `next` from the second call only. After one click, what does the first line say?
hint: How many `monday` refs were made?

choices.text: Plan: 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-01, the same as the review
choices.why: That is a store's behaviour. Each call to `useWeek` makes a `monday` of its own, so the second week moving does not move the first.
Right. The first call has its own `monday` ref, and nothing touched it.

choices.text: Plan: 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-01, because both calls were given the same start date
choices.why: The same argument is not the same state. The function ran twice and made two refs, whatever it was given.

choices.text: Nothing: the two calls fight over one ref, and Vue warns
choices.why: There is no conflict to warn about. Two calls, two refs; the capture shows both lines printed.

prompt: Why is `const { monday, sunday, next } = useWeek('2026-10-19')` safe, when destructuring a `reactive` object is not?
hint: Look at what each piece is.

choices.text: The template keeps whatever it is given reactive, destructured or not
choices.why: The template unwraps refs; it cannot bring back reactivity to a plain value read once in the script.

choices.text: `useWeek` returns `reactive({ … })`, which hands out refs when destructured
choices.why: That describes `toRefs`, not `reactive`. A reactive object loses its reactivity when destructured, which is why `useWeek` returns a plain object.

choices.text: A week changes rarely, so reading it once is close enough
choices.why: The review line moved to the 26th after a click, so it did follow the change; nothing was read once.

choices.text: Each piece it returns is a ref or a function
choices.why: Right. Destructuring copies the references, and a ref copied is still the same ref.

prompt: Which of these did turning `WeekPager` into `useWeek` buy? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare a component in the tree with a function call.

choices.text: No extra component in the tree
choices.why: Right. A composable is a function call; nothing is rendered for it.

choices.text: Two independent weeks in one component, from two calls
choices.why: Right. A renderless component would have to be written twice in the template for that.

choices.text: A single week shared by every component that calls it
choices.why: Each call makes fresh state. Shared state is a store, and that is lesson 13.

choices.text: A test that calls it as a function, with nothing mounted
choices.why: Right. Lesson 21 does exactly that.

choices.text: Faster updates, since a composable works outside Vue's reactivity
choices.why: It works through Vue's reactivity: `ref` and `computed` are the whole of `useWeek`.

prompt: In the `Conventions` demo, why did the line from `useHours(minutes.value)` stay at 1.50 after the click?
hint: What did that call actually pass?

choices.text: `toValue` reads a ref once, the first time it is called, and caches it
choices.why: `toValue` reads the ref every time the `computed` runs; the ref line moved to 2.00 through the same function.

choices.text: A composable sees changes made during setup, and the click came after it
choices.why: The ref and the getter both followed the click, which came after setup too.

choices.text: It was handed 90, and a number cannot change
choices.why: Right. `minutes.value` is read once, at the call, and what arrives is a plain number.

choices.text: Its `computed` kept its first result until the component was mounted again
choices.why: A `computed` recomputes when what it read changes. This one read nothing reactive, so there was nothing to change.

prompt: `___(input)` gives back the value of a ref, the result of a getter, or a plain value as it is, so a composable need not care which it was handed.
hint: It is imported from `vue`, and `useHours` calls it.

prompt: A composable returns `reactive({ data, error, loading })`, and a component writes `const { data } = useIt()`. What happens when the data arrives?
hint: Lesson 2 destructured a reactive object.

choices.text: The component's `data` was read once and stays at what it was
choices.why: Right. Destructuring read the property once; a plain object of refs would have handed out a ref instead.

choices.text: Vue refuses: a reactive object cannot be destructured
choices.why: Destructuring works without a word from Vue; what is lost is the link, which is why it goes unnoticed.

choices.text: The new data shows, because `reactive` hands each property out as a ref
choices.why: That is `toRefs(…)`. Plain `reactive` gives out the current value, which no longer follows the object.

choices.text: `data` follows, but `error` and `loading` lose their reactivity
choices.why: All three are the same kind of property on the same object; destructuring treats them alike.

prompt: Before writing a general composable, for the window's size or the mouse, where does the lesson say to look first?
hint: A collection written to these conventions.

choices.text: Pinia
choices.why: Pinia is the store of lesson 13: shared state, not a collection of small composables.

choices.text: TanStack Query, which keeps answers by address
choices.why: That library is for fetching with a cache; the lesson names it for that and nothing else.

choices.text: VueUse
choices.why: Right. Some two hundred composables, written to the same conventions as this lesson's.

choices.text: The `vue` package itself, which ships one per browser API
choices.why: `vue` ships the pieces, `ref`, `computed`, the hooks, and no composable for the window or the mouse.

prompt: In `useFetchJson`, which read decides when the `watchEffect` runs again?
hint: Tracking stops at the first `await`.

choices.text: `toValue(url)`, which the effect reads on its very first line
choices.why: Right. It is the one reactive read before the first `await`, and the lesson put it there on purpose.

choices.text: `loading.value`, which each run sets to true
choices.why: Setting a ref is a write, not a read, and a write does not make the effect depend on it.

choices.text: Everything it touches, `await response.json()` included
choices.why: Whatever runs after the first `await` is outside the tracking window, so it adds nothing.

choices.text: `data.value`, which is assigned when the answer arrives
choices.why: That assignment comes after the `await`, and it is a write; neither would make it a dependency.

prompt: The course changes to Spanish while the statistics request is still on its way. What does `useFetchJson` do with the statistics request?
hint: Follow `onWatcherCleanup`, then the `catch`.

choices.text: Waits for it to finish, then starts the Spanish one
choices.why: The `watchEffect` reruns at once; the cleanup is what deals with the old run, and it does not wait.

choices.text: Aborts it; that run logs `gave up on` and returns, leaving `error` alone
choices.why: Right. An aborted request is not an error the user should see, so the `catch` drops it.

choices.text: Aborts it, and shows `Could not load: AbortError` until Spanish answers
choices.why: The `catch` checks for `AbortError` first and returns before setting `error`.

choices.text: Lets it finish, then throws away its answer
choices.why: That is the flag of lesson 4. Here an `AbortController` stops the request itself.

prompt: Asking for `/notes/nope.json` showed `Unexpected token '<'` rather than a 404. Why?
hint: What did the dev server send back?

choices.text: The server sent the HTML page, and parsing it as JSON failed
choices.why: Right. The address does not exist, the dev server answered with the page, and the composable reported what that caused.

choices.text: `response.ok` was false, but it is checked only after `response.json()`
choices.why: The check comes first in `useFetchJson`, and for a 404 it would have thrown `404 Not Found`.

choices.text: The request was aborted halfway, leaving half a document
choices.why: An abort is caught and logged as `gave up on`; it never reaches the screen.

choices.text: `useFetchJson` turns every 404 into a JSON error so that the screen has one message to show
choices.why: A non-ok answer throws its own status; nothing turns one error into another.

prompt: In the capture, after how many ticks was each `TickerUser` stopped?
hint: The two `stopped after` lines.

prompt: `tooLate()` calls `useTicker('called from a click')` from a button. What happens?
hint: Which component is being set up at that moment?

choices.text: A timer starts and is never stopped, since nothing is removed
choices.why: The timer is started inside `onMounted`, and that callback was never registered, so no timer exists to leak.

choices.text: The hooks attach to `LifecycleInside`, whose handler made the call
choices.why: Hooks attach to the component being set up, not to the one whose code is running; `LifecycleInside`'s setup was over.

choices.text: Vue warns once per hook, and no timer starts
choices.why: Right. With no component being set up, `onMounted` and `onUnmounted` had nothing to attach to.

choices.text: Vue throws, and the button stops responding
choices.why: It is a warning, `[Vue warn]`, and the page goes on working.

prompt: `useTicker` is called from each of these places in a component. Which calls give its hooks a component to attach to? Choose all that apply.
hint: Is the component still being set up when the line runs?

choices.text: At the top level of `<script setup>`
choices.why: Right. That is the place the rule names.

choices.text: Inside a `setTimeout` started during setup
choices.why: The callback runs after setup has finished, so there is no component being set up.

choices.text: Inside an `if` at the top level of `<script setup>`
choices.why: Right. Setup is still running, and in Vue a condition does not matter.

choices.text: Inside the `.then()` of a `fetch` started during setup
choices.why: The `.then()` runs when the answer arrives, long after setup.

choices.text: In a click handler, as `tooLate` does
choices.why: That is the capture's own example: two warnings and no timer.

prompt: How often does a composable's body run for one component that calls it?
hint: Setup, or every render?

choices.text: On every render of that component
choices.why: That is a React custom hook. A Vue component's setup runs once, and the composable with it.

choices.text: Each time one of the refs it returned changes
choices.why: A ref changing reruns what depends on it, a `computed` or the template; it does not rerun the function that made it.

choices.text: Once per interpolation in the template that reads it
choices.why: The template reads the refs; it never calls the composable.

choices.text: Once, during the component's setup
choices.why: Right. Which is why its functions are created once, and nothing needs `useCallback`.

prompt: Why may a composable be called inside an `if` in setup, when a React hook may not be called inside one?
hint: How does each framework find a piece of state again?

choices.text: Vue's compiler moves every composable call out of its condition
choices.why: Nothing is moved; the call stays where it was written, and runs only if the condition holds.

choices.text: Vue finds the state by the ref objects, not by the order of the calls
choices.why: Right. Setup runs once and the refs are ordinary objects the component holds; React matches state to the position of each hook call on each render.

choices.text: Vue runs setup again on every render in the same order
choices.why: Setup runs once. If it ran on every render, the order would matter in Vue too.

choices.text: Vue has the same rule and just does not warn about it
choices.why: The table says a condition is allowed, and the reason is that nothing in a composable depends on order.

prompt: In a React hook, a derived value is wrapped in `___` with a list of dependencies written by hand; in a composable, `computed` finds its own.
hint: The React counterpart of `computed`.

prompt: Which of these stayed in `App.vue` when the two composables took over?
hint: What only `App` can decide.

choices.text: The `watch` that saves the sessions to local storage
choices.why: Saving moved into `usePlannerData`, with the loading, because they are one job.

choices.text: The `monday` ref, which says which week is on show
choices.why: Right. Which week is shown is the screen's decision, so it stays with the screen.

choices.text: The timer that keeps `today` current
choices.why: The timer and its two hooks went into `useToday`.

choices.text: The `STORAGE_KEY` constant
choices.why: It lives beside the code that uses it, in `usePlannerData.js`.

prompt: Lesson 12's course page also calls `usePlannerData()`. A session is ticked in `App`. What does the course page show?
hint: What does every call to a composable make?

choices.text: The tick, at once, since both calls read the same storage key
choices.why: They share a key in storage, not a list in memory; storage is read once, when the data loads.

choices.text: A warning that the composable is already used by `App`
choices.why: Vue has no notion of a composable being in use; the second call is a second ordinary function call.

choices.text: A list of its own, which lacks the tick until the page is reloaded
choices.why: Right. Two calls, two lists, two watchers writing over each other's copy: shared state needs one owner.

choices.text: The tick, because `usePlannerData` keeps one cached answer per address
choices.why: That cache belongs to libraries like TanStack Query. This composable fetches again on every call.

prompt: A colleague from React wraps the `previous` and `next` that a composable returns in a memo helper, so that they are not recreated. What does that buy in Vue?
hint: How many times are those functions created?

choices.text: Fewer re-renders of the component, as in React
choices.why: In React the memo keeps a child from re-rendering on a new function; in Vue the function was never new.

choices.text: The refs they change stay reactive, which they would otherwise not
choices.why: The refs are reactive whatever wraps the functions that change them.

choices.text: It lets the template call them in a `@click`
choices.why: `TwoWeeks` calls `next` in a `@click` with no wrapper at all.

choices.text: Nothing: they were created once, during setup
choices.why: Right. A composable runs once, so there is no re-render to fear.

prompt: `useNotes(course)` fetches a course's notes. A component calls `useNotes(course.value)`, and the notes never follow a change of course. Which fix follows the lesson's conventions?
hint: What should the component pass, and what should the composable do with it?

choices.text: Call `useNotes(course.value)` again inside a `watch` on `course`
choices.why: That is a composable called after setup: its watchers and hooks would have no component to attach to.

choices.text: Make `useNotes` return `reactive({ … })` instead of refs
choices.why: The output was not the problem. The input arrived as a plain string, and no return type brings back what was never passed.

choices.text: Pass `course`, or `() => course.value`, and read it with `toValue` inside a watcher
choices.why: Right. Pass the ref or a getter, and the composable follows it, as `useFetchJson` follows its address.

choices.text: Wrap `course.value` in `ref()` at the call
choices.why: `ref(course.value)` is a new ref holding a copy; changing `course` does not change it.
